When a dog is suddenly surprised, its brain triggers an instant survival mode called the 'Fight or Flight' response. The Amygdala (the brain's emotional center) sends a quick distress signal, releasing Adrenaline. This causes the dog to jump or run away rapidly to stay safe, even before it fully understands what happened. It’s a natural and healthy way their brain protects them!

video_api_description:
This is Sundari’s last journey.

This video is not for sympathy—this is for awareness. If you choose to raise a small, innocent life, then do everything it takes to protect them, no matter what.

Because of the Holi gap, there was a delay of 2–3 days in her treatment. She was suffering from Parvo, and those days cost me everything. If Holi hadn’t come in between, maybe Sundari would still be in my arms today.

I want to say this clearly—I did everything I could to save her. I tried my best, gave my all, and never gave up on her. This wasn’t a lack of love or care… it was a situation that went out of my control.

Still, as a pet parent, this pain will stay with me forever. I may never be able to forgive myself.

Please learn from this—never ignore even the smallest symptoms. Act immediately. Sometimes, even a little delay can change everything.

Sundari was not just my pet, she was my baby. And I will carry her in my heart forever. 💔

When the zombie apocalypse finally arrives—not with sirens, but with a suspicious silence—you quickly realize that all survival guides lied, because you are standing in your kitchen holding nothing but a spoon and the crushing responsibility of your own decisions. Slowly, the chaos outside fades into background noise as you realize survival isn’t about strength or weapons, but about staying calm, staying quiet, and respecting the absurd fact that a spoon and basic intelligence might actually be enough to outlast the end of the world.

Use the spoon as a mirror, a noise-maker, and an emotional support object
If a place looks scary, don’t enter it (this is common sense, please)
Avoid malls, hospitals, and anywhere zombies would logically go first
Walking quietly > running dramatically
If you drop the spoon, accept your fate internally but retrieve it carefully
Zombies hear panic; calm people survive longer
Lock doors, block exits, and never trust a “quick look”

The ways dad jokes differ from other jokes and indeed other forms of humor can be telling. (Humor researchers caution us most earnestly that if we dare to dissect why a joke is even funny, it'll take all the humor out of it. But since dad jokes are mostly not very funny anyway, I think we can take a chance).

What Makes a Joke Funny?
On the face of it we may think of jokes as fun and games, a way to make others laugh from delight and surprise. Humor has been shown to bring people closer socially and relieve the stress of negative situations. Jokes have an undeniable power to reveal truths and create a rapport.

Then again, Freud famously argued that jokes were a socially acceptable form
 of hostility and aggression. Successful joke telling can form a bond between the teller and the audience, but sometimes they are banded together against the of the joke. It turns out the social forces that drive our use of jokes, while they may improve our moods, aren't always a laughing matter.

Topics that are usually too inappropriate to discuss in certain polite circles can be comedy gold to others: people falling and hurting themselves; people's personal traits such as weight, height, hair color, or ethnicities; even taboo or subjects. Jokes can reinforce conservative, conventional views of what's considered normal."The racist can safely broach a taboo subject by making a nasty remark cloaked in humor-that is, to use humor as a testing device," notes Peter Farb. The listener can show whether they find it acceptable by laughing, or not.

What makes a thing funny? At its core, humor seems to be all about incongruity. Comic situations set up a context where something is marked or out of place. This oddness, far different to what we were led to expect or what we blithely assume is normal, is what makes things funny. The joke par excellence has to be cleverly original, yet not too clever that no one can get it. Telling a good joke needs a delicate balance.

Successful jokes, especially when new to the listener, can increase the social status of the teller in the hierarchy of a group, allowing them control over the social interaction. If you're a good comedian, people are going to give you more opportunities to tell jokes. The performance of joke telling actually usurps the normal turn-taking customs of conversation by reserving the right to speak and forcing listeners to play along with the format of the joke (for example in a knock-knock joke or riddle). For the time of the joke, it's an exercise in defining a reality that is "fiercely conservative," according to some researchers, maintaining our conventional views of the world by laughing at what's different. laughter you laugh you lose

The ways dad jokes differ from other jokes and indeed other forms of humor can be telling. (Humor researchers caution us most earnestly that if we dare to dissect why a joke is even funny, it'll take all the humor out of it. But since dad jokes are mostly not very funny anyway, I think we can take a chance).

What Makes a Joke Funny?
On the face of it we may think of jokes as fun and games, a way to make others laugh from delight and surprise. Humor has been shown to bring people closer socially and relieve the stress of negative situations. Jokes have an undeniable power to reveal truths and create a rapport.

Then again, Freud famously argued that jokes were a socially acceptable form
 of hostility and aggression. Successful joke telling can form a bond between the teller and the audience, but sometimes they are banded together against the butt of the joke. It turns out the social forces that drive our use of jokes, while they may improve our moods, aren't always a laughing matter.

Topics that are usually too inappropriate to discuss in certain polite circles can be comedy gold to others: people falling and hurting themselves; people's personal traits such as weight, height, hair color, or ethnicities; even taboo or sexual subjects. Jokes can reinforce conservative, conventional views of what's considered normal."The racist can safely broach a taboo subject by making a nasty remark cloaked in humor-that is, to use humor as a testing device," notes Peter Farb. The listener can show whether they find it acceptable by laughing, or not.

What makes a thing funny? At its core, humor seems to be all about incongruity. Comic situations set up a context where something is marked or out of place. This oddness, far different to what we were led to expect or what we blithely assume is normal, is what makes things funny. The joke par excellence has to be cleverly original, yet not too clever that no one can get it. Telling a good joke needs a delicate balance.

Successful jokes, especially when new to the listener, can increase the social status of the teller in the hierarchy of a group, allowing them control over the social interaction. If you're a good comedian, people are going to give you more opportunities to tell jokes. The performance of joke telling actually usurps the normal turn-taking customs of conversation by reserving the right to speak and forcing listeners to play along with the format of the joke (for example in a knock-knock joke or riddle). For the time of the joke, it's an exercise in defining a reality that is "fiercely conservative," according to some researchers, maintaining our conventional views of the world by laughing at what's different. laughter you laugh you lose

About Taarak Mehta Ka Ooltah Chashmah:
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The show is inspired from the famous humorous column 'Duniya Ne Undha Chasma' written by the eminent Gujarati writer Mr. Tarak Mehta. This story revolves around daily happenings in "Gokuldham Co-operative Society" and covers topical issues which are socially relevant. The show predominantly - revolves around 'Jethalal' who is an uneducated Gujarati businessman. Your 'Taarak Mehta', is his neighbor. 'Jethalal' finds a friend and philosopher in 'Taarak Mehta' and often goes to him for advice whenever he is in trouble. Jethalaal's family includes his simpleton wife 'Daya Ben' and a mischievous son 'Tapu'. Tapu is a menace and a constant source of trouble to all the members of Gokuldham. They have often warned 'Jethalal' to reform 'Tapu' or else be prepared to leave the premises. Lost hopes of being heard by his son push Jethalal' to call his father 'Champaklal' from the village. This was his great idea of leashing some control over the mischievous Tapu. The opposite happens and the grandfather joins hands with the grandson to make life a roller coaster troublesome ride for Jethalal.

About Taarak Mehta Ka Ooltah Chashmah:
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The show is inspired from the famous humorous column 'Duniya Ne Undha Chasma' written by the eminent Gujarati writer Mr. Tarak Mehta. This story revolves around daily happenings in "Gokuldham Co-operative Society" and covers topical issues which are socially relevant. The show predominantly - revolves around 'Jethalal' who is an uneducated Gujarati businessman. Your 'Taarak Mehta', is his neighbor. 'Jethalal' finds a friend and philosopher in 'Taarak Mehta' and often goes to him for advice whenever he is in trouble. Jethalaal's family includes his simpleton wife 'Daya Ben' and a mischievous son 'Tapu'. Tapu is a menace and a constant source of trouble to all the members of Gokuldham. They have often warned 'Jethalal' to reform 'Tapu' or else be prepared to leave the premises. Lost hopes of being heard by his son push Jethalal' to call his father 'Champaklal' from the village. This was his great idea of leashing some control over the mischievous Tapu. The opposite happens and the grandfather joins hands with the grandson to make life a roller coaster troublesome ride for Jethalal.

About Taarak Mehta Ka Ooltah Chashmah:
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The show is inspired from the famous humorous column 'Duniya Ne Undha Chasma' written by the eminent Gujarati writer Mr. Tarak Mehta. This story revolves around daily happenings in "Gokuldham Co-operative Society" and covers topical issues which are socially relevant. The show predominantly - revolves around 'Jethalal' who is an uneducated Gujarati businessman. Your 'Taarak Mehta', is his neighbor. 'Jethalal' finds a friend and philosopher in 'Taarak Mehta' and often goes to him for advice whenever he is in trouble. Jethalaal's family includes his simpleton wife 'Daya Ben' and a mischievous son 'Tapu'. Tapu is a menace and a constant source of trouble to all the members of Gokuldham. They have often warned 'Jethalal' to reform 'Tapu' or else be prepared to leave the premises. Lost hopes of being heard by his son push Jethalal' to call his father 'Champaklal' from the village. This was his great idea of leashing some control over the mischievous Tapu. The opposite happens and the grandfather joins hands with the grandson to make life a roller coaster troublesome ride for Jethalal.

video_description: George Carlin delivers a sharp stand-up riff on the phrase “proud to be an American,” arguing that pride should come from something earned rather than from luck of birth. video_introduction: Funniest Sketch Ever?
label: Comedy Skits
video_description: In this British comedy sketch, a nervous officer and two soldiers carefully handle an unexploded mortar round or bomb while treating the dangerous task with absurdly calm, overelaborate instructions, debating which part to touch, joking about colors and warning lights, and inching the detonator out with exaggerated caution; the tension builds as they fuss over the device like it is a routine repair, then breaks into darkly deadpan humor when one of them suggests sorting it out and even going for a drink, turning a life-or-death situation into a perfectly straight-faced military farce.
video_api_description: My favourite sketch from The Fast Show
comment_1: I was in the infantry. I spent two years with 81mm mortars. If the round misfired there were two ways of very gently removing the faulty round from the tube. One way used a tool called a ‘knacker-knasher’, which was dropped down the tube until its teeth engaged in a recess on the round. The other method involved detaching tube from the baseplate, tilting the tube on its bipod legs until the round slid out into your hands. A bit like the removal of the detonator in the sketch. Once the faulty round had been extricated from the tube it was handed to a Royal Engineers Ammunitions Technical Officer (ATO) who would then unceremoniously hurl the thing a few feet into the back of a 4-tonner where the round clattered around one floor with other munitions!! This sketch reminds me of that. 😊
comment_2: "Either we all die or get a drink. Win win"
comment_3: No, and it's beat by a bomb scene from MASH:  "The instructions say "Cut the red Wire...(snip)...but first, cut the blue wire".
comment_4: Almost Fell off my seat laughing at this so British it's brilliant
comment_5: From the second golden age of British comedy. Anyone who was offended had to just get over it.

video_introduction: This is one of the funniest comedy sketches ever!!
label: Comedy Skits
video_description: A quiet British-style comedy sketch follows a man in a dark coat and hat as he spots a banknote trapped beneath an orange Beetle on a busy street, then fusses over how to reach it while drifting in and out of a nearby cafe and back to the curb. With almost no dialogue, the scene builds through careful gestures, repeated attempts, and deadpan reactions, turning an ordinary bit of street business into a smooth, slow-burn gag that ends with a satisfying surprise.
video_api_description: This is one of the funniest comedy sketches of all time. From BBC. Starring Irish comedian named Dave Allen, the sketch was aired in the 70`s or 80`s on the BBC.
comment_1: There is something about these types of skits that make it just that much classier. No words spoken, smooth, slow, but so perfect

comment_3: Would've been even funnier if it turned out the cafe owner had set this up each time.  :D
comment_4: Now seriously, I didn't expect that!
comment_5: I was half expecting that the restaurant had placed this car on the money, to attract business. 😂. This was way funnier than I thought.

video_introduction: Coffee Name | Comedy Sketch | Awkward Cafe Misunderstanding
label: Comedy Skits
video_description: In a busy cafe, a shy customer tries to order a black coffee and is asked for a name, which sparks an increasingly awkward misunderstanding as he assumes the barista wants his own name for the drink and keeps suggesting absurd options like “Mr. Blacky” before the exchange spirals into a ridiculous debate about names and race; the scene ends with the barista playfully labeling the cup “Jon Whitey,” turning the whole order into an uncomfortable but sharp comedy skit.
video_api_description:
A short comedy on unconscious bias and the fear white folk have of causing offense, especially using the word "black" in front of black people. This comedy sketch was inspired by a barista asking me this exact question (but not in a Starbucks).

For more hilarious Comedy Skits visit http://skittell.com 



The Gas Station

A comedy skit featuring a customer who supplies discount vouchers to lower his petrol cost -- yet is still unsatisfied with the service.

This is an example of a short and sharp two person comedy skit featuring a customer and cashier at a local gas station.  The scene is established early with an external shot showing a car and petrol bowsers, before moving inside to reveal interaction between customer and cashier.

comment_1:
For anyone who is confused, shoving Greg normally doesn't do anything when he's a vendor. However, because of an oversight it's possible to trick the game into thinking Greg is a companion for a two frame window by what we call "double-dialog-skip", where you use mouse and keyboard shortcuts simultaneously to skip dialog.

Once Greg has been pushed, you need to enter the space he was stood in. This is technically out of bounds so the game will then try to push the player into a valid space, and here we take advantage of Bucket Launch.

The bucket in Honeywood is coded to only have collision on the inside, so by placing a bucket on your head you create unintended collision and the game can't put you back into play. It will keep trying until you eventually build up a crazy speed value that eventually hurls you a considerable distance.

Being hurled into the sky wouldn't normally be useful so this exploit went ignored for years, but in September 2022 we discovered Comet Skip, and that changed everything...

video_introduction: Tommy Cooper's Birthday Speech for Prince Philip
label: Daily Life Jokes
video_description: At a formal royal dinner celebrating Prince Philip’s birthday, Tommy Cooper delivers a gloriously absurd, deadpan routine that turns a polite speech into a masterclass in comedy. He opens with a string of playful misunderstandings about being “a man or a mouse,” jokes about elephants being frightened of mice, and then wanders through mock-serious remarks about the occasion before launching into a card trick that only deepens the chaos. With his rumpled tuxedo, oversized stage presence, and perfectly timed nonsense, he keeps the audience laughing while pretending to treat everything with complete sincerity, capturing the unique charm that made him one of Britain’s most beloved comedians.
video_api_description: Another short clip of the legendary Tommy Cooper.

video_introduction: How the English language would sound if silent letters weren’t silent - BBC
label: Talk Shows / Stand-Up Comedy / Cross-Talk
video_description: A BBC stand-up routine on a red-curtain stage takes a playful swing at English spelling by imagining what the language would sound like if every silent letter were pronounced, turning ordinary words like hour, subtle, knight, champagne, lasagna, and scissors into absurd versions of themselves. The comedian builds the joke into a mock celebration of “silent letter day,” complete with invented customs, food, and gifts, while the crowd laughs at how much of English is really a patchwork of old spellings and borrowed words that no longer match the way they’re spoken.

video_introduction: Stand-up Comedy Advice: 4 Mistakes I See at Every Comedy Open Mic...

video_introduction: Indian Insults & Comebacks | Stand-up Comedy by Abhishek Upmanyu
label: Talk Shows / Stand-Up Comedy / Cross-Talk
video_description: Abhishek Upmanyu delivers a sharp stand-up routine about how Indians handle insults by instantly repeating them, turning offense into a sarcastic comeback, and how this behavior carries into family life, where parents recycle the same words with added attitude. He riffs on conservative parents, awkward jokes about sexuality, Indian ignorance around homosexuality, and the way fathers and families respond to everything with deadpan practicality, from birth and health to career pressure and morning routines. The set blends observational comedy with fast, chaotic wordplay, while the audience reacts loudly throughout, especially to the jokes about middle-class life, Indian dads, and the familiar habit of telling children to wake up early and “set life right.”

video_introduction: I Dance, You Dance, He Dances. Does He Dance More Than Me? I Don't Think So. Verbs in English.

video_description: A comedian on stage turns English verb conjugation into a joke, repeating “I dance, you dance, he dances” and then playfully stretching the grammar to absurdity as he asks whether “he dances” more than “me.” Holding a microphone against a brick-wall comedy-club backdrop, he leans into the confusion between correct English and broken phrasing, speaking in a mock-foreign accent and building the bit around simple verbs, bad grammar, and exaggerated confidence. video_introduction: Silent Letter Day
label: Talk Shows / Stand-Up Comedy / Cross-Talk
video_description: A stand-up comedian delivers a sharp, fast-paced routine about the absurdity of silent letters in English, joking that words like hour, subtle, knife, gnome, champagne, and queue are full of letters that seem to exist only to cause trouble. video_introduction: ISMO Leikola - English Is So Messed Up
label: Talk Shows / Stand-Up Comedy / Cross-Talk
video_description: Finnish comedian Ismo Leikola delivers a sharp, energetic stand-up routine about the absurdities of English, riffing on how hard it is to learn as a second language and turning everyday phrases into clever wordplay. He jokes about discovering favorite words, using sounds as a Wi‑Fi password, mocking vague corrections like “language,” and dismantling tongue-twisters such as “she sells seashells by the seashore” with a businessman’s eye for bad location. The set builds on his precise timing and playful delivery, keeping the audience with him as he turns linguistic confusion into a fast, confident, and highly entertaining performance.

video_introduction: Basketball Scene - SNL
label: Talk Shows / Stand-Up Comedy / Cross-Talk
video_description: In a chaotic SNL basketball scene, a coach tries to stage an emotional conversation with a talented player about missing tryouts and squandering a possible scholarship, but the shoot repeatedly falls apart as the background extras keep turning the moment into an absurd pickup game. Between the director’s shouted resets, the players dribbling, passing, hugging, and fumbling their way through the scene, the cast keeps missing marks and drifting into comedy, with one extra even proudly mentioning a “sports movement class at Juilliard.” The sketch builds into a running disaster of bad basketball, broken concentration, and escalating frustration, turning a serious sports-movie setup into a goofy behind-the-scenes meltdown.
